newsitem.title: UK: BTPs shine, Canadian debt stumbles in week-Salomon.
newsitem.headline: BTPs shine, Canadian debt stumbles in week-Salomon.

text.p: Italian BTPs outstripped other government bond markets for the second week in a row while Canadian debt brought up the rear this week, according to data from Salomon Brothers on Friday.
Overall, the the Salomon Brothers World Government Bond Index (WGBI) showed a meagre gain of 0.02 percent in local currency terms and 0.07 percent in dollar terms in the week to June 26.
BTPs racked up a return of 0.75 percent in lira terms and 0.71 percent in dollar terms as optimism over European convergence trades led the market higher.

In second place was the British gilt market which offered investors a return of 0.63 percent in sterling terms despite muted trade ahead of the budget on July 2. Gilts led the way in dollar terms with a 1.84 percent improvement.

Of the other major European bond markets, Denmark managed a gain of 0.61 percent in local currency terms, France 0.55 percent and Belgium 0.54 percent. The Netherlands and Germany gained 0.53 and 0.51 percent respectively.

The dollar bloc countries and Japan fared less well with all four making losses on the week in local currency terms. Canada was the worst performing market, suffering a 0.59 percent loss in local terms, but managing a 0.06 percent gain in U.S. dollar terms.
The Bank of Canada surprised markets by raising its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.5 percent on Thursday -- the first move by the bank since it cut rates 25 basis points on November 8, 1996.

Japanese government bonds saw a 0.51 percent loss in yen terms and a 0.34 percent loss in dollar terms after the market took a hit on a stronger-than-expected Tankan survey. T-bonds showed a 0.28 percent loss.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
